title: PostgreSQL Window Functions
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on SQL window functions in PostgreSQL: the OVER clause, partitions, ordering and frames, ranking, offset and value functions, running aggregates, filtering results, and performance with indexes.

chapters.title: Window Functions: The Big Idea
points: A window function computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (its window) without collapsing rows
GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group; a window function keeps every input row and adds a column
Syntax shape: function(args) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame_clause)
Empty OVER () means the window is the entire result set
Any aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) becomes a window function when followed by OVER
Example: SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER () AS company_avg FROM emp; shows each row beside the global average
Example: salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) gives each person's gap versus their department
Window functions are only allowed in the SELECT list and ORDER BY, not in WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING or FROM
Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT output, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Window functions see rows after WHERE and HAVING filtering, so filtered-out rows never enter a window
Use cases: ranking, top-N per group, running totals, period-over-period change, percent of total, gaps and islands

chapters.title: OVER, PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
points: PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups; the function restarts in each partition
Omitting PARTITION BY makes the whole result one partition
ORDER BY inside OVER sorts rows within each partition and defines what 'previous' and 'current' mean
The ORDER BY inside OVER is separate from the query's final ORDER BY and does not guarantee output order
Adding ORDER BY to an aggregate window silently changes it from whole-partition to running (default frame)
SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g) gives the group total on every row; SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d) gives a running total
PARTITION BY accepts expressions, e.g. PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
Multiple partition columns: PARTITION BY region, product creates one window per combination
ORDER BY supports DESC, ASC, NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST; NULLs sort last in ASC by default in PostgreSQL
Ranking functions require ORDER BY to be meaningful; ROW_NUMBER with no ORDER BY gives arbitrary numbering
Mistake: forgetting the outer ORDER BY and assuming rows come back in window order
Percent of total pattern: amount / SUM(amount) OVER () * 100

chapters.title: Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
points: ROW_NUMBER() gives unique sequential integers 1,2,3... even for ties
RANK() gives tied rows the same rank and then skips numbers: 1,2,2,4
DENSE_RANK() gives tied rows the same rank with no gaps: 1,2,2,3
Scores 90,85,85,70: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4; RANK 1,2,2,4; DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3
ROW_NUMBER takes no arguments and needs a deterministic ORDER BY, otherwise ties are numbered arbitrarily
Add a unique tiebreaker (ORDER BY score DESC, id) to make ROW_NUMBER repeatable
Top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) then keep rn <= 3
Use RANK or DENSE_RANK when ties should all qualify, ROW_NUMBER when you need exactly N rows
Deduplication: keep rn = 1 per key ordered by updated_at DESC
PERCENT_RANK() = (rank - 1) / (rows - 1) and CUME_DIST() = rows at or before / total rows
Mistake: using ROW_NUMBER for 'top 3 salaries' and silently dropping tied people
Ranking functions ignore the frame clause; they only use partition and ORDER BY

chapters.title: LAG, LEAD and Offset Navigation
points: LAG(expr, offset, default) reads a value from a previous row in the partition; LEAD reads from a following row
Defaults: offset 1, default value NULL when the target row does not exist
LAG(price, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY day) substitutes 0 for the first row instead of NULL
Day-over-day change: price - LAG(price) OVER (ORDER BY day)
Percent growth: (rev - LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY m)) / NULLIF(LAG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0)
LAG(x, 7) compares to the same weekday last week; LEAD(x, 3) peeks three rows ahead
LAG and LEAD ignore the frame; they count rows from the current row within the partition
Always include PARTITION BY when data holds many entities, or LAG leaks across customers
Time between events: ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)
Missing calendar rows make 'previous row' differ from 'previous day'; generate_series a calendar first
Gaps and islands: compare id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) to group consecutive runs
Mistake: no ORDER BY inside OVER makes LAG nondeterministic

chapters.title: Frames: ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS
points: A frame is the subset of the partition, relative to the current row, that an aggregate or value function sees
Syntax: {ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS} BETWEEN frame_start AND frame_end
Bounds: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, N PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, N FOLLOWING, UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
ROWS counts physical rows: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is exactly three rows
RANGE works on ORDER BY values and includes all peers (rows with equal ORDER BY value) of the current row
RANGE with offsets (value PRECEDING) needs exactly one numeric, date or interval ORDER BY column: RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
GROUPS (PostgreSQL 11+) counts peer groups: GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW; without ORDER BY it is the whole partition
Peer effect: with ties on the ORDER BY key, the default RANGE frame gives tied rows the same running total
Use ROWS for a predictable running total and for speed, as RANGE must track peers
EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, EXCLUDE GROUP, EXCLUDE TIES and EXCLUDE NO OTHERS (default) trim the frame
Shorthand: ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Mistake: RANGE offsets on a text or multi-column ORDER BY raise an error

chapters.title: Running Totals and Moving Averages
points: Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
Per-group running total: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY ts ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
3-row moving average: AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Centered average: ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
7-day trailing average by calendar: AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ROWS averages count rows, so gaps in dates distort a '7-day' average; RANGE respects real dates
The first rows have fewer than N rows in the frame; the average uses what exists, so mask with CASE WHEN row_number >= N
Running count: COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
Running min and max: MAX(price) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) gives the all-time high so far
Running share: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) / SUM(x) OVER ()
Aggregates over a sliding frame use inverse transition functions where available, so SUM and COUNT slide in O(1) per row
Mistake: ties in ORDER BY with the default RANGE frame produce repeated running totals instead of stepping

chapters.title: FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE and NTILE
points: FIRST_VALUE(x) returns x from the first row of the frame; LAST_VALUE(x) from the last row of the frame
NTH_VALUE(x, n) returns the nth row of the frame, or NULL if the frame is smaller
LAST_VALUE pitfall: the default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so it just returns the current row's own value
Fix: add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
Or avoid LAST_VALUE by using FIRST_VALUE with the opposite ORDER BY direction
NTH_VALUE has the same default-frame trap; second highest needs the full frame
FIRST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY day) compares every price to the launch price
IGNORE NULLS and FROM LAST are SQL standard options that PostgreSQL does not support; emulate with subqueries or a FILTER trick
NTILE(n) splits an ordered partition into n buckets numbered 1..n
NTILE bucket sizes differ by at most one: 10 rows into 4 buckets gives 3,3,2,2
NTILE(4) gives quartiles, NTILE(100) approximates percentiles; ties can land in different buckets
Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) for a true median, since NTILE is only bucketing

chapters.title: Named WINDOW Clause and Reuse
points: WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) is declared after HAVING and before the final ORDER BY
Reference it with OVER w to avoid repeating the same spec
Example: SELECT RANK() OVER w, SUM(salary) OVER w FROM emp WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)
Several named windows are comma separated: WINDOW w1 AS (...), w2 AS (...)
A window can extend another: OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Rule: the child cannot repeat PARTITION BY and can add ORDER BY only if the base has none
The base window cannot have a frame clause when you extend it
Window definitions in the same query must be declared before use only logically; order in WINDOW list does not matter for references
Equivalent windows are computed in one sort and one WindowAgg pass, so naming does not change performance, only readability
Different OVER specs create separate WindowAgg nodes, each possibly with its own sort
Align windows to share PARTITION BY and ORDER BY prefixes so the planner can reuse one sort
Named windows keep dashboards of running totals and ranks consistent and less error-prone

chapters.title: Filtering Window Results and QUALIFY Alternatives
points: WHERE cannot reference a window function because windows run after WHERE
PostgreSQL has no QUALIFY clause (Snowflake, BigQuery, Teradata do)
Pattern 1, subquery: SELECT * FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) rn FROM t) s WHERE rn = 1
Pattern 2, CTE: WITH r AS (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (...) rk FROM t) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rk <= 3
Pattern 3, DISTINCT ON: SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) * FROM t ORDER BY user_id, ts DESC returns the latest row per user
DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL specific, concise and often faster than ROW_NUMBER for one row per group
Pattern 4, LATERAL: FROM users u, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.uid = u.id ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 3) top3
LATERAL with an index can beat a window scan when there are few groups needed from many
Filtering before the window (WHERE inside the subquery) changes the window contents; filtering after does not
Mistake: putting a filter inside the subquery when you wanted the rank computed over all rows
Mistake: HAVING SUM(x) OVER () is invalid unless the window runs over grouped output
Window over aggregates: SELECT dept, SUM(x), RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(x) DESC) FROM t GROUP BY dept

chapters.title: Performance, Indexes and Cheatsheet
points: EXPLAIN shows a WindowAgg node, usually fed by a Sort on (PARTITION BY cols, ORDER BY cols)
A btree index on (partition_col, order_col) lets the planner skip the sort with an Incremental or index scan
Match index column order and direction to PARTITION BY then ORDER BY
Multiple windows with different sort keys need multiple sorts, so order them to share a prefix
WindowAgg processes partitions in a streaming fashion, but large partitions with frame offsets can spill to disk
Sort uses work_mem; raise it per session for big windows and watch for 'Sort Method: external merge'
Reduce rows first: filter with WHERE and project only needed columns before the window
Top-1 per group at scale: DISTINCT ON or LATERAL with LIMIT can avoid sorting everything
Run-condition optimization (PostgreSQL 15+) stops WindowAgg early for ROW_NUMBER() <= N style filters on the outer query
Cheatsheet: ranking = ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK; offset = LAG/LEAD; value = FIRST/LAST/NTH_VALUE; bucket = NTILE
Cheatsheet: default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW with ORDER BY, whole partition without
Cheatsheet: use ROWS for running totals, explicit full frame for LAST_VALUE, subquery or DISTINCT ON to filter
